issues.legal_issue: An employer that hires services for the benefit of its employees may qualify as a consumer in respect of those services.
material_facts: The trust acquired housing construction services by taking possession of flats and paying consideration.
The trust intended to provide accommodation in the flats to nurses employed by its hospital.
issues.conclusion: The trust, as the hirer of the housing services for the benefit of its employees, could claim consumer status in respect of the transaction.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(1)(d)(ii) of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 includes a hirer of services and, where services are availed of with the hirer’s approval, their beneficiary. In Spring Meadows Hospital v. Harjol Ahluwalia, (1998) 1 CPJ 1 (SC), the Court held that a person who hires services for a beneficiary may be a consumer. The same principle applies where an employer hires services for the welfare of its employees.

predicates.consumer_service_dispute: A dispute concerns services hired for consideration and a claim to consumer status in relation to those services.
predicates.employer_hired_service: An employer hired services for consideration.
predicates.service_intended_for_employee_beneficiar: The employer hired the services for the benefit of its employees.

issues.definition: When an employer hires services for its employees in a consumer service dispute, the employer may qualify as a consumer for that transaction.

issues.legal_issue: Housing services acquired to provide employee accommodation are not for a commercial purpose when their dominant purpose is employee welfare and they have no close and direct nexus with profit-generating activity.
material_facts: The trust acquired the flats to accommodate nurses employed by its hospital, rather than to provide medical or diagnostic facilities.
The flats were provided to the nurses without rent.
There was no claim that the trust earned a surplus from the flats or engaged in buying and selling flats.
Any improvement in hospital efficiency or income from providing accommodation was indirect and conjectural.
issues.conclusion: The purchase of the flats was not for a commercial purpose, so the trust was a consumer for this transaction. The appeal was allowed, and the complaint was restored before the National Commission for decision on its merits.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 2(1)(d) of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, whether a transaction is for a commercial purpose is a question of fact. Laxmi Engineering Works v. P.S.G. Industrial Institute, (1995) 3 SCC 583, explains that the self-employment Explanation clarifies rather than exhausts the definition and that the purpose for which goods or services are used matters. Synco Textiles Pvt. Ltd. v. Greaves Cotton and Company Limited, (1991) 1 CPJ 499, and Paramount Digital Colour Lab v. Agfa India Private Limited, (2018) 14 SCC 81, emphasize the need for a close nexus between the transaction and large-scale profit-making activity. The dominant purpose, rather than the purchaser’s identity or transaction value, is relevant; personal use or use for a beneficiary, or a purpose otherwise unlinked to commercial activity, need not satisfy the self-employment test. Employee-welfare services would not usually be commercial merely because they may indirectly improve productivity. The Court distinguished Kalpavruksha Charitable Trust v. Toshniwal Brothers (Bombay) Pvt. Ltd., (2000) 1 SCC 512, where equipment had a direct nexus with the operation of a diagnostic centre.

rule.if: consumer_service_dispute and service_purchased_for_employee_welfare and (no_direct_nexus_to_profit_activity or dominant_purpose_is_beneficiary_welfare) and no_direct_profit_from_transaction

predicates.consumer_service_dispute: A dispute concerns whether a person who acquired services for consideration may claim consumer status.
predicates.service_purchased_for_employee_welfare: An employer acquired the service to provide a welfare benefit to its employees.
predicates.no_direct_nexus_to_profit_activity: The service was not directly used in the employer’s profit-generating operations.
predicates.dominant_purpose_is_beneficiary_welfare: The dominant purpose of acquiring the service was the personal use or welfare of the employees who benefited from it.
predicates.no_direct_profit_from_transaction: The employer did not directly earn profit from the acquired service.

issues.definition: If an employer acquires a service principally for employee welfare, without directly using it in profit-generating activity or earning profit from it, the employer is a consumer for that transaction.
